question: You've deployed containers to ECR/EKS before, but conceptually, what problem does Kubernetes actually solve that plain Docker doesn't?
answer_html:
Docker gives you a way to package and run a single container, but it doesn't answer questions like: what happens when the host machine dies, how do I run five copies of this container across multiple machines, and how does traffic find the right copy when containers restart and get new IP addresses. Kubernetes is an orchestrator that takes a fleet of machines and a set of container images and continuously works to make the running state match a desired state you declare.

Concretely, it handles scheduling (deciding which machine runs which container), self-healing (restarting or rescheduling containers that die or fail health checks), scaling (running more or fewer copies), service discovery (giving a stable name/IP to a group of pods whose individual IPs change constantly), and rolling updates (replacing old versions with new ones without downtime).

In your EKS experience, you were mostly interacting with the parts of Kubernetes that do this for you already -- Deployment objects handling rollouts, Service objects handling stable networking. The interview will likely probe what's happening underneath those abstractions.

question: What is a Pod, and why doesn't Kubernetes just run containers directly?
answer_html:
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It's a wrapper around one or more containers that are guaranteed to be scheduled on the same node, share the same network namespace (so they can reach each other on localhost), and can share storage volumes. Most pods you've deployed on EKS probably had exactly one container, which is the common case.

The reason Kubernetes doesn't schedule bare containers is that some workloads genuinely need tightly coupled helper processes -- for example a sidecar container that ships logs, or an init container that runs setup logic before the main app starts. Grouping them into one Pod means they always live and die together and share networking, which would be awkward to guarantee with independent containers.

Pods are also treated as disposable. You almost never create a Pod directly in production; instead you create a higher-level object like a Deployment, which creates and manages Pods for you and replaces them when they fail.

question: What's the difference between a Deployment and a Service? People conflate these a lot.
answer_html:
A Deployment and a Service solve two completely different problems, and the confusion usually comes from the fact that you almost always create one of each together.

  • A Deployment manages compute: it declares how many replicas of a Pod should run, rolls out new versions of your container image, and replaces Pods that crash or get evicted. Under the hood a Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, which is the object actually responsible for keeping N pod replicas alive at any given time.
  • A Service manages networking: it gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to a group of Pods selected by label, so that other things in the cluster have one consistent address to call even as the underlying Pods are replaced, rescheduled, or scaled up and down.

Without a Service, a Deployment's Pods would still work, but every consumer would need to track individual Pod IPs that change on every restart -- which is unworkable at any real scale.

question: Walk me through the difference between control-plane components and worker-node components. Where does your EKS experience stop?
answer_html:
A Kubernetes cluster is split into a control plane (the brain, making decisions) and one or more worker nodes (where your actual application containers run). On EKS, AWS manages the control plane for you entirely -- you never see it, which is exactly why this is a knowledge gap worth closing before an interview that expects on-prem/hybrid administration.

Control-plane components:

  • kube-apiserver -- the front door; every kubectl command and every internal component talks to the cluster only through this REST API.
  • etcd -- a distributed key-value store that is the single source of truth for all cluster state (every object you've ever created lives here).
  • kube-scheduler -- decides which node a new Pod should run on, based on resource requests, constraints, and node availability.
  • kube-controller-manager -- runs the reconciliation loops (controllers) that notice drift between desired and actual state and correct it, e.g. the ReplicaSet controller creating a replacement Pod after one dies.

Worker-node components:

  • kubelet -- the agent on each node that talks to the API server, and actually starts/stops/monitors containers via the container runtime.
  • kube-proxy -- programs networking rules on the node so traffic sent to a Service's virtual IP gets routed to one of the correct backing Pods.
  • Container runtime (e.g. containerd) -- the low-level software that actually pulls images and runs containers, invoked by the kubelet.

On EKS you interact with the worker-node layer (your Pods run there) and the API through kubectl, but AWS owns etcd, the API server, the scheduler, and the controller-manager for you. In a self-managed or on-prem cluster, all of that becomes your responsibility -- which is the gap this prep is closing.

question: What are the different Service types, and when would you use ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer?
answer_html:
A Service's type field controls how it's exposed:

  • ClusterIP (the default) -- gets a stable virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster. This is what you use for internal service-to-service traffic, e.g. a backend API talking to a database Pod's Service.
  • NodePort -- in addition to a ClusterIP, opens a static port (in the 30000-32767 range by default) on every node's IP. Anything that can reach any node on that port gets routed to the Service. It's mostly a building block other things use, or a quick way to expose something on-prem without a cloud load balancer.
  • LoadBalancer -- asks the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer (e.g. an AWS NLB/ELB) that forwards traffic to a NodePort under the hood. This is the common way to expose a service to the internet on EKS, which is likely what you've used without necessarily seeing the NodePort layer beneath it.

There's also ExternalName, which just returns a DNS CNAME with no proxying involved, used to alias an external service into cluster-internal DNS.

A key interview point: a Service is not a process or a load balancer instance running somewhere -- it's a networking rule (a set of iptables/IPVS entries programmed by kube-proxy on every node) plus a DNS entry. There's no single place it "runs."

question: If Services already exist, why do we also need Ingress?
answer_html:
A LoadBalancer Service gives you one external IP/load balancer per Service. If you have ten HTTP services, that's potentially ten cloud load balancers, and no shared logic for routing by hostname or URL path. Ingress solves that by giving you a single entry point that does HTTP/HTTPS-aware routing -- rules like "requests to api.example.com/users go to the users Service, api.example.com/orders goes to the orders Service" -- all behind one load balancer.

An important nuance: an Ingress object by itself does nothing. It's just a set of routing rules; you need an Ingress controller (e.g. NGINX Ingress Controller, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Traefik) actually running in the cluster to watch Ingress objects and configure a real proxy or cloud load balancer to implement them. If you create an Ingress and nothing happens, the most likely cause is that no controller is installed or watching that ingressClassName.

Ingress also commonly handles TLS termination, so certificates live in one place rather than being managed per-Service.

question: What is a CNI plugin, and what's its role in a cluster's networking?
answer_html:
CNI (Container Network Interface) is a specification, and a CNI plugin (e.g. Calico, Cilium, Flannel, the AWS VPC CNI used on EKS) is the actual software that implements pod networking. When the kubelet starts a Pod, it calls the CNI plugin to assign that Pod an IP address and wire up its network interface so it can talk to other Pods.

Kubernetes itself defines a networking model with a few hard requirements but no built-in implementation: every Pod gets its own IP, Pods can reach all other Pods across the whole cluster without NAT, and a Pod sees its own IP the same way others see it. The CNI plugin is what actually delivers on those guarantees -- typically via some combination of virtual bridges, overlay networks (VXLAN), or, in the case of the AWS VPC CNI, by directly attaching real VPC-routable ENI IPs to Pods so pod traffic looks like normal VPC traffic.

This matters for troubleshooting: if Pods can't reach each other at all (not just Service traffic, but raw Pod-to-Pod), the CNI plugin and its node-level agent (e.g. a calico-node or aws-node DaemonSet pod) is usually where you start looking, not the Service or kube-proxy layer.

question: How does DNS resolution actually work inside a cluster? What happens when a pod calls another service by name?
answer_html:
Kubernetes runs an internal DNS service, almost always CoreDNS, as a set of Pods managed by a Deployment in the kube-system namespace, fronted by its own Service (commonly named kube-dns). Every Pod's /etc/resolv.conf is automatically configured by the kubelet to point at that CoreDNS Service's ClusterIP as its nameserver.

Every Service automatically gets a DNS record of the form <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, which resolves to that Service's ClusterIP. Within the same namespace you can just use <service-name>; across namespaces you need <service-name>.<namespace>. So when a Pod calls http://payments-api, the resolver appends the search domains from resolv.conf, queries CoreDNS, gets back the payments-api Service's ClusterIP, and the request proceeds from there -- DNS resolution and Service routing are two separate steps.

This is a very common failure point: if a Pod can resolve a name but the connection then times out, the problem is downstream of DNS (Service/endpoints/network policy). If it can't resolve the name at all, check that CoreDNS Pods are Running and that the Pod's resolv.conf points at the right ClusterIP -- kubectl exec into the pod and run a DNS lookup, or check CoreDNS's own logs with kubectl logs.

question: What's the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret, and between readiness and liveness probes?
answer_html:
A ConfigMap and a Secret both let you inject configuration into a Pod (as environment variables or mounted files) without baking it into the container image. The difference is intent, not real encryption by default: a Secret's values are base64-encoded rather than plaintext in the object, and Kubernetes applies some extra precautions around them (e.g. not printing values in kubectl describe output, optional encryption-at-rest in etcd if configured). Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so a Secret is not secure by itself -- for real secret management most production setups add etcd encryption at rest and often an external secret store (e.g. AWS Secrets Manager via an integration), rather than relying on Secret objects alone.

Probes are how the kubelet checks on container health, and mixing them up is a very common mistake:

  • Liveness probe -- answers "is this container stuck/dead?" If it fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. Get this wrong (too aggressive) and you cause self-inflicted CrashLoopBackOffs on an app that was just slow, not broken.
  • Readiness probe -- answers "should this Pod currently receive traffic?" If it fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's endpoints (so no traffic is routed to it) but the container is not restarted. This is what you want during startup warm-up, or temporary downstream dependency issues.

A pod stuck failing readiness will show as Running but never receive traffic -- a scenario worth remembering for networking troubleshooting questions.

question: A Service isn't routing traffic to its pods -- clients get connection refused or timeouts. Walk me through your debugging process, step by step.
answer_html:
This is a classic interview scenario because it forces you to reason layer by layer instead of guessing. A methodical approach:

  • 1. Confirm the Pods are actually healthy. kubectl get pods -o wide -- are they Running and, specifically, READY (passing their readiness probe)? A Pod can be Running but 0/1 Ready, which means it's intentionally excluded from traffic.
  • 2. Check the Service has Endpoints. kubectl get endpoints <service-name> (or EndpointSlices). If this list is empty, the Service's label selector doesn't match the Pods' labels -- by far the most common root cause of this exact symptom. Compare kubectl get svc <name> -o yaml's selector against kubectl get pods --show-labels.
  • 3. Check the port mapping. Confirm the Service's targetPort actually matches the port the container is listening on inside the Pod, not just the Service's external port. A mismatch here gives you connection refused even with correct Endpoints.
  • 4. Test connectivity progressively closer to the source. From another Pod, curl the Pod IP directly (bypasses the Service and kube-proxy entirely -- tests raw Pod-to-Pod/CNI networking). Then curl the Service's ClusterIP (tests kube-proxy's rules). If the Pod IP works but the ClusterIP doesn't, the problem is in kube-proxy/iptables/IPVS on that node, not the app.
  • 5. Check for a NetworkPolicy silently blocking traffic. kubectl get networkpolicy -A -- a policy scoped to the target Pod's labels may be denying ingress from the caller.
  • 6. Use kubectl describe svc and kubectl describe pod for events, and check kube-proxy's own logs/mode (iptables vs IPVS) if everything above looks correct but traffic still doesn't land.

The key interview signal is going in order from "is anything actually wrong at the Pod level" outward to Service, to node networking, to policy -- rather than jumping straight to blaming the network.

question: How does NetworkPolicy work, and why might two teams' policies conflict in ways that are hard to spot?
answer_html:
By default, Kubernetes networking is flat and open: any Pod can talk to any other Pod across the whole cluster, with no isolation. A NetworkPolicy is how you restrict that, but two things trip people up immediately: it only takes effect if the CNI plugin supports it (not all do -- e.g. plain Flannel historically didn't, while Calico and Cilium do), and policies are additive/whitelisting, not a simple allow/deny toggle.

The mental model: as soon as any NetworkPolicy selects a given Pod for a given direction (ingress or egress), that direction becomes default-deny for that Pod, and only traffic matching some policy's rules is allowed through. If no policy selects a Pod at all, that Pod remains fully open in that direction.

Conflicts happen in a few classic ways:

  • Multiple policies, intersecting scope. Policies are additive (union of allows), so two teams each writing a narrow policy for the same Pod won't "fight" each other in the sense of one blocking what the other allows -- but a team assuming their policy is the only one in effect can be surprised when traffic they didn't explicitly allow still gets through because another policy already opened it.
  • Missing DNS egress. A very common self-inflicted outage: someone locks down egress for a Pod to "only the database," forgetting to also allow egress to CoreDNS (typically UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system). The Pod can no longer resolve any name, including the one it's supposed to talk to.
  • Namespace-scoped assumptions. A policy allowing ingress "from the same namespace" silently breaks when another team's Pods that need access live in a different namespace, and there's no obvious error -- just timeouts.

Debugging these usually means listing every NetworkPolicy that selects the affected Pod (kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns> -o yaml) and manually reasoning through whether the specific traffic direction and port is covered by at least one rule.

question: What role does etcd play in the cluster, and what's involved in upgrading nodes -- things you'd never have touched on EKS?
answer_html:
etcd is a distributed, consistent key-value store, and it is the single source of truth for the entire cluster's state -- every object (Pods, Deployments, Secrets, everything you've ever applied) is stored there. The API server is the only component that talks to etcd directly; everything else (scheduler, controllers, kubelet) reads and writes cluster state exclusively through the API server, which persists it to etcd. If etcd is down or its data is corrupted, the cluster's control plane effectively stops functioning even if all your application Pods are still running fine on worker nodes.

Because it's the source of truth, etcd needs regular backups (etcdctl snapshot save) and, in a self-managed or on-prem setup, runs on an odd number of nodes (3 or 5) for quorum -- losing more than half the etcd members loses write availability for the whole cluster. On EKS, AWS runs and backs up etcd for you; on-prem or self-managed clusters (e.g. via kubeadm), this becomes something you're directly responsible for.

Node upgrades follow a similar "never seen on EKS" pattern. The standard approach, one node at a time:

  • Cordon the node (kubectl cordon) so the scheduler stops placing new Pods on it.
  • Drain it (kubectl drain), which evicts existing Pods so they get rescheduled elsewhere, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets where defined.
  • Upgrade the node's kubelet/kube-proxy/OS packages (or, for a control-plane node run via kubeadm, run kubeadm upgrade steps first).
  • Uncordon the node so it can receive Pods again, then move to the next node.

Control-plane nodes are typically upgraded one at a time in the same cordon/drain pattern to avoid ever losing etcd or API-server quorum simultaneously across multiple members.
